title: The Memorial Consequences of Multiple-Choice Testing https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03194051
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), January 15, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton's summary of Marsh, Roediger, Bjork, and Bjork's paper examines the double-edged nature of multiple-choice testing: it boosts later performance through the testing effect, but it can also plant false facts in students' memories, especially when the wrong answer was arrived at through reasoning rather than a guess. The paper finds that the overall benefit of testing outweighs this downside, but that errors students reason their way into are more likely to stick than errors from random guessing. Multiple-choice questions can also activate and cue prior knowledge that a student didn't realize they had, and can teach genuinely new facts when students use elimination reasoning to land on the correct answer. The authors recommend mitigations including immediate feedback, offering a 'don't know' option with a penalty for wrong guesses, and varying question types across assessments, though switching to higher levels of Bloom's taxonomy alone doesn't change the balance of positive versus negative effects. The core message is that tests don't just measure knowledge — they actively modify it, for better and for worse.
points: Errors that come from a student's own flawed reasoning are more likely to persist in memory than errors that come from random guessing, so teachers should watch for reasoning-based mistakes in particular.
The positive testing effect reliably outweighs the negative misinformation effect overall, but immediate feedback and a penalised 'don't know' option both measurably reduce the downside.
Multiple-choice tests can teach students genuinely new correct facts through elimination reasoning, not just assess what they already know.

Switching to higher-cognitive-level (Bloom's taxonomy) questions does not by itself change the ratio of positive to negative testing effects — the mechanism is about reasoning and feedback, not question difficulty.
quotes: While testing generally improves later performance (the testing effect), it also introduces students to incorrect answers. The study reveals that students may learn and retain these false facts, particularly those arrived at through reasoning rather than guessing.

Multiple-choice tests provide retrieval practice: Tests help students retrieve information, and this practice strengthens memory. The answer options in multiple-choice tests can also serve as retrieval cues, which helps students recall information.
Multiple-choice tests can teach new facts: Students can learn new facts from multiple-choice tests by using reasoning to eliminate lures and select the correct answer.

Errors that result from reasoning are more likely to persist: Errors that students make when they use reasoning or personal experience to justify their answer are more likely to persist than errors that are the result of guessing.
Consider using a “don't know” option: Providing a “don't know” option, along with a penalty for selecting wrong answers, can reduce the production of incorrect answers in later tests.
The overall positive effect of testing…outweighs any negative consequences
